subject: Two-stage count model, ML, or Bayesian for multi-species point count data?

messages.author: e485a3be8a302512
messages.subject: Two-stage count model, ML, or Bayesian for multi-species point count data?
parts:
Dear DS community, 
I want to assess the impact of farming practice and of small-scale habitat/native vegetation patches on the abundance of ~100 bird species (for some analyses expressed in relation to their abundances in the forest). I'm trying to figure out how information can best be shared between species and get the most precise estimates. 
In occupancy modelling, a Bayesian approach is very common, but seems to be less so for distance sampling (- is there a reason for this?). I take from this blog (Model-based inference analysis from Buckland et al. (2015) (distancesampling.org)) that I ultimately have three options (two-stage count model, maximum likelihood, or Bayesian) but I struggle to find what would be most suitable in my case.

I have 25 forest squares, 13 natural farming squares, and 13 chemical farming squares. Each square is 500m x 500m and contains 4 systematically arranged point count locations, 200m apart and 150m from the square edge. I visited each point count 4 times: winter 2022, summer 2022, winter 2023, summer 2023. The natural & chemcial farming squares span a gradient in the percentage of habitat patches embedded in the square. I counted all bird species I saw or heard, so that's a bit over 100 species. Whilst some were very common, others (especially forest specialists) were rare.

Initially, I was planning on conducting a two-stage count model: For species with at least 40 observations, I'd fit species-specific detection functions. For those with fewer observations, I'd group species into detectability groups based on taxonomic, dietary, and behavioural characteristics (obtained from AVONET). For each species or group, I'd then fit detection functions where I'd consider three models for each species or species group: a detection function with (1) land use type (farming vs forest) as a covariate, (2) the proportion of closed habitat (surrounding each point) as a covariate, and (3) no covariates. In each case, I'd test the following key functions and adjustments half-normal and hazard-rate with cosine adjustment, half-normal with hermite polynomial adjustment, and hazard-rate with simple polynomial adjustment. For the group-level detection functions, I'd include species as a covariate in each model. I'd then fit linear mixed models to the observed count data, seperately for each species, with the estimated effective area as an offset and a nested random effect with square identity as a random term and farming practice and the percentage of habitat patches as predictor variables (and using bca bootstrapping to get CIs).
(I'd then also fit bird density-crop yield functions, seperately for each farming practice for each species following Phalan et al 2011, where forest is zero yielding). 

However, I feel that information is not shared as effectively between species as it could (should?) be when it comes to estimating square-level density for each species & modelling the effect of farming pratice & habitat patches. I am thus wondering whether a ML or Bayesian approach would give me more precision in my estimates (ie increase my ability to detect effects if there are any) and/or save me time, but I am unsure of how to find out whether either of them would be suitable and how this code could be best updated for multiple species (presumably by adding species as a random term as well as some trait characteristics?).

Some guidance on this would be greatly appreciated. I haven't found any examples of the ML or Bayesian approach in a similar context.

Many thanks,
Iris
